THOUGHT: The patient is an older woman with multiple annular erythematous crusted plaques on the trunk with peripheral pustular collarettes. There is a history of recurrent intertriginous outbreaks (axillae, groin) previously treated topically. Histology shows prominent suprabasal acantholysis described as a “dilapidated brick wall” with a neutrophil-rich serous crust in the stratum corneum. Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) is negative for immunoreactants. Staphylococcus aureus was isolated from the pustular exudate.

Key points linking findings:
- The clinical pattern (crusted, collarette pustules, annular plaques on trunk) and positive S. aureus culture point toward a bacterial (staphylococcal) process such as bullous impetigo / staphylococcal epidermolytic toxin–mediated cleavage. Staphylococcal cleavage of desmoglein-1 can produce superficial acantholysis that mimics pemphigus histologically but will have a negative DIF because it is not autoimmune.
- The histologic description of widespread suprabasal acantholysis (“dilapidated brick wall”) is classically seen in pemphigus group disorders (pemphigus vulgaris or superficially in some pemphigus foliaceus variants). However, autoimmune pemphigus typically gives a positive intercellular IgG/C3 on DIF — which is absent here, arguing against classic autoimmune pemphigus.
- IgA pemphigus and subcorneal pustular dermatosis (Sneddon–Wilkinson) can present with annular pustular plaques and neutrophil-rich subcorneal pustules; DIF in IgA pemphigus would show IgA intercellular deposition (negative here), and microbiology is typically sterile (whereas this culture grew S. aureus).
- Pemphigus vulgaris would usually show suprabasal clefts with tombstoning and mucosal disease and a positive DIF — features that are not present clinically or by DIF.

Putting these together, an infectious staphylococcal process (bullous impetigo / staphylococcal toxin–mediated superficial blistering mimicking pemphigus) best explains the combination of pemphigus-like histology with negative DIF and a positive S. aureus culture. Autoimmune pemphigus variants, IgA pemphigus, and Sneddon–Wilkinson remain important differentials but are less likely given the negative DIF and culture result.

DIAGNOSIS:
1) Bullous impetigo / staphylococcal toxin–mediated superficial blistering (staphylococcal infection mimicking pemphigus) — most likely given positive S. aureus culture, crusted annular/pustular collarette lesions, and non‑autoimmune (DIF negative) acantholysis.
2) Pemphigus foliaceus (superficial pemphigus) — clinicopathologically similar (superficial crusting, annular plaques); histology can be compatible, but strongly argued against by negative DIF and positive bacterial culture.
3) IgA pemphigus (subcorneal pustular dermatosis type) — fits annular pustular plaques and neutrophil-rich subcorneal pustules; less likely because DIF for IgA was negative and bacterial culture was positive.
4) Subcorneal pustular dermatosis (Sneddon–Wilkinson) — clinical pattern and neutrophilic subcorneal pustules fit, but usually sterile pustules and DIF negative; culture positivity favors an infectious cause over sterile dermatosis.
5) Pemphigus vulgaris — histology can show suprabasal acantholysis, but the absence of mucosal involvement and a negative DIF make classic PV unlikely.

A healthy woman in her 60s presented with multiple erythematous crusted plaques on her trunk that had appeared 4 weeks previously, sparing her limbs and facial region. She had a long-standing history of several outbreaks of skin lesions limited to both axillae and groin. Previous episodes had been successfully treated with various topical drugs administered by her primary care physician. No family history of similar lesions was recorded.

Physical Examination:
Multiple annular erythematous plaques surrounded by a peripheral crusted and pustular collarette on her trunk. No active lesions were present in her axillae, inframammary folds, or groin.

A mild inflammatory infiltrate was identified on superficial papillary dermis.- Direct immunofluorescence:  Results: Negative for IgG, IgA, IgM, fibrin, and complement deposition- Microbiological culture:  Results: Staphylococcus aureus isolated from pustular exudate- Clinical Images:  Image Title: Multiple erythematous and crusted plaques  Image Description: Diffusely distributed on the dorsal trunk at presentation    Image Title: Erythematous annular plaque  Image Description: Surrounded by a crusted and focally pustular peripheral collarette
